title: Federal Judge Blocks FEMA's 50% Staffing Cut: 'Pulled From Thin Air'
summary:
A federal judge has ruled that a Homeland Security plan to cut the Federal Emergency Management Agency's staff by 50% was unlawful — a victory for labor groups who sued to stop it.

U.S. District Judge Susan Illston issued her opinion late Friday. She wrote that top Homeland Security officials late last year directed FEMA's leadership to submit a staffing plan including a 50% cut, even though the agency's own supervisors objected. "Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air," Illston wrote.

The judge said the government violated rules established after 2005's Hurricane Katrina. Those rules put decisions on FEMA staffing squarely in FEMA's hands, not the Department of Homeland Security's, and prevented DHS from "substantially" reducing FEMA's functions.

The issue was part of a much larger lawsuit filed by the American Federation of Government Employees and other labor groups, pushing back on the Trump administration's efforts to slash the federal workforce. The Department of Homeland Security was then led by Secretary Kristi Noem. DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

FEMA said in a statement that while it does not comment on personnel matters or ongoing litigation, "DHS and FEMA are ready for the 2026 hurricane season." It said it is "ensuring workforce stability and a strong, deployable force" and making the agency "leaner, faster and laser-focused" on supporting state, local, tribal and territorial partners.

Although FEMA has experienced terminations, the 50% cuts ultimately were not carried out. In recent months, after leadership changes at FEMA and DHS, the agency has rehired some staffers who were let go.

Illston did not order a specific remedy. She directed the two sides to meet and decide on a course of relief. The ruling comes as FEMA has been buffeted by mass departures, disruptions of grant programs and delays of disaster aid. An August report from the Government Accountability Office found that the departures of thousands of staff in 2025 resulted in a "loss of institutional knowledge and experienced personnel."
why_it_matters: Disaster agencies are the backstop millions of people depend on in the worst weeks of their lives, so lawsuits like this decide how quickly a president can reshape that backstop — and whether courts or agency experts get the final say over who is protected.

background_read: The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) was created in 1979 to coordinate the U.S. government's response to disasters, and it was folded into the Department of Homeland Security when that department was set up after the September 11 attacks. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 overwhelmed the agency and exposed how weak it had become, so Congress passed the Post-Katrina Emergency Management Reform Act of 2006, which gave FEMA more independence inside DHS and made it harder to strip away its duties — the rules Judge Susan Illston (a federal district judge in California who has served since the 1990s) relied on.

The American Federation of Government Employees (the largest union for U.S. federal workers) has repeatedly sued over efforts to shrink the civil service, and the Government Accountability Office (an independent agency that audits federal programs and reports to Congress) supplies the numbers those fights turn on.

Kristi Noem (the former governor of South Dakota who became Secretary of Homeland Security) led DHS when the staffing plan was ordered, and FEMA's own supervisors objected to the 50% figure at the time. Some conservative policy groups argue that FEMA should be shrunk or even abolished and that states should handle more of their own disaster response.

perspectives.description: They see the ruling as proof that the post-Katrina protections still work: staffing decisions belong with the people who run emergency response, not with political appointees. For them, a FEMA stripped of half its staff would mean slower help when hurricanes and floods hit.

perspectives.perspective: Supporters of a smaller federal government
perspectives.description: They argue FEMA has grown bloated and that a leaner agency, with more responsibility pushed to states, would respond faster and cost less. Some also question whether judges should be dictating how an executive agency is organised, and an appeal is possible.

They note a pattern: after huge failures like Katrina, the U.S. tends to strengthen and protect its disaster agency, then later tries to shrink it again. The case is really one battle in a larger struggle over the federal workforce and presidential control of agencies, with the GAO's findings on lost expertise as hard evidence of the practical costs.

The judge left the remedy open, so what happens next depends on negotiations between the government and the unions. Watch whether rehiring continues, whether the ruling is appealed, and how FEMA performs in the 2026 hurricane season — the agency's own stated test of readiness.
